claims.text: Controlled in-situ precipitation of nanoscale coherent secondary phases in refractory HEAs can improve strength, ductility, and toughness without sacrificing high-temperature or irradiation stability.
The baseline refractory HEA consists of high-melting refractory elements.
The baseline alloy has a single-phase or multiphase polycrystalline structure.
The baseline alloy has inherently good thermal and irradiation stability.
A tailored thermal or thermomechanical treatment can induce homogeneous nanoscale lattice-matched intermetallic precipitates within the primary BCC matrix.
Processing conditions can be tailored to control precipitate size, distribution, and volume fraction.
Lattice-matched coherent precipitates will exhibit minimal coarsening or phase segregation during prolonged high-temperature and irradiation exposure.
The coherent precipitates will impede dislocation motion through Orowan-type strengthening.
The precipitates may act as stable sinks for irradiation-induced defects.
Defect-sink behavior of the precipitates will help preserve microstructural integrity during thermal and irradiation exposure.
The precipitate-engineered alloy will have higher yield strength than the baseline alloy.
The precipitate-engineered alloy will have greater ductility than the baseline alloy.
The precipitate-engineered alloy will have greater toughness than the baseline alloy.
The precipitate-engineered alloy will not exhibit accelerated precipitate coarsening or other microstructural degradation under high-temperature and irradiation conditions.
Refractory HEAs without engineered coherent nanoprecipitates lack the additional reinforcement supplied by a dispersed nanoscale secondary phase.
Mechanical benefits depend on careful control of precipitate volume fraction and size distribution.
Excessive precipitation, precipitate coarsening, or inappropriate lattice mismatch may eliminate the mechanical gains and compromise thermal or irradiation stability.
